gloss: A heavy iron block that a blacksmith hammers hot metal on.
examples: The blacksmith laid the glowing bar on the *anvil*.
Old *anvils* sell for a lot at farm auctions.
In the cartoon, an *anvil* falls out of the sky.

gloss: A system of laws that keeps racial groups apart and gives one of them all the power.
examples: South Africa ended *apartheid* in the early 1990s.
She grew up under *apartheid* and later wrote about it.
The museum documents daily life during *apartheid*.
contrast: The h is silent: say uh-PAR-tayt (or uh-PAR-tite), never uh-PART-hide.

gloss: The opening in a camera lens that lets light through, or any narrow opening.
examples: Open the *aperture* wider if the room is dark.
Both lenses have a maximum *aperture* of f/1.8.
Light came through a narrow *aperture* in the wall.

gloss: A short sentence that states a general truth.
examples: He ended every lecture with the same *aphorism*.
The book is a collection of *aphorisms* about work.
"Less is more" is a famous *aphorism*.

gloss: A food or drug believed to increase sexual desire.
examples: Oysters have a reputation as an *aphrodisiac*.
None of these so-called *aphrodisiacs* work.
Power, he joked, is the best *aphrodisiac*.

gloss: Calm confidence in a difficult situation.
examples: She handled the hostile questions with *aplomb*.
He answered the reporters with surprising *aplomb*.
The waiter cleaned up the spill with complete *aplomb*.
contrast: The b is silent: uh-PLAHM.

gloss: A condition in which breathing stops for short periods, usually during sleep.
examples: His doctor thinks he has sleep *apnea*.
The machine treats *apnea* by keeping the airway open.
Untreated *apnea* can raise your blood pressure.
contrast: Americans write *apnea*; the British write *apnoea*.

gloss: A ghost, or a figure that appears suddenly and strangely.
examples: She swore she saw an *apparition* on the stairs.
The old inn is famous for its *apparitions*.
In the fog he looked like an *apparition*.

gloss: The policy of giving in to an aggressive country to avoid a fight.
examples: Critics called the deal pure *appeasement*.
The 1930s taught Europe the cost of *appeasement*.
He denied that the talks were *appeasement*.

gloss: A part that sticks out from a larger body, or something added on and less important.
examples: A crab uses its front *appendages* to grab food.
The garage looks like an *appendage* to the house.
The committee became a useless *appendage* of the board.

gloss: Cooked apples mashed into a soft, sweet food.
examples: The kids eat *applesauce* with almost everything.
We serve pork chops with *applesauce*.
You can use *applesauce* instead of oil in the recipe.
contrast: *Applesauce* is uncountable: say *some applesauce* or *a jar of applesauce*, never *an applesauce*.

gloss: A small tool used to put a liquid or cream onto something.
examples: The polish comes with a foam *applicator*.
Throw the used *applicators* in the trash.
Squeeze the tube and spread it with the *applicator*.

gloss: A person who has been given a job or position by someone in power.
examples: The governor's newest *appointee* takes office Monday.
Several *appointees* resigned after the scandal.
He was a political *appointee*, not a career official.

gloss: Someone whose job is to decide what property is worth.
examples: The bank sent an *appraiser* to look at the house.
Two *appraisers* came up with very different numbers.
She works as an *appraiser* for an insurance company.

gloss: A feeling of worry that something bad is about to happen.
examples: She opened the letter with some *apprehension*.
There is real *apprehension* about the layoffs.
He watched the storm approach with growing *apprehension*.

gloss: A way of dealing with a problem or a task.
examples: Her *approach* to teaching is very hands-on.
We tried three different *approaches* before one worked.
The company needs a fresh *approach* to hiring.

gloss: Official permission, or the feeling that something is good.
examples: The plan still needs *approval* from the city council.
He looked at his father for *approval*.
The drug won federal *approval* last spring.

gloss: A natural ability to learn or do something well.
examples: She has a real *aptitude* for languages.
The school gives an *aptitude* test in ninth grade.
The job matches his *aptitudes* almost perfectly.
contrast: Americans say AP-tih-tood; the British add a y sound: AP-tih-tyood.

gloss: A bridge or channel built to carry water over a long distance.
examples: A Roman *aqueduct* still stands outside the town.
The city gets its water through a hundred-mile *aqueduct*.
Several *aqueducts* were damaged in the earthquake.

gloss: A layer of rock or sand underground that holds water.
examples: Farmers here pump water from a deep *aquifer*.
The *aquifer* is dropping about a foot a year.
Fertilizer runoff has polluted two *aquifers*.

gloss: A person or body with the power to settle a dispute or decide what is correct.
examples: The court is the final *arbiter* of the Constitution.
Magazines used to be the *arbiters* of taste.
Both sides agreed to accept the *arbiter*'s decision.

gloss: Buying something in one market and selling it in another to profit from the price difference.
examples: The fund made most of its money on *arbitrage*.
Fast computers have squeezed the profit out of *arbitrage*.
He spent ten years doing currency *arbitrage*.
contrast: The ending sounds French — AR-bih-trahzh — not like the -age in *garbage*.

gloss: An angel of the highest rank.
examples: The painting shows an *archangel* with a sword.
Michael and Gabriel are the best-known *archangels*.
A stone *archangel* stands over the church door.
contrast: Here ch sounds like k — ARK-ayn-jul — but in *archbishop* and *archer* it is the ch of *church*.

gloss: A bishop of the highest rank, in charge of a large church region.
examples: The *archbishop* spoke at the memorial service.
Two *archbishops* signed the open letter.
He was named *archbishop* of Chicago in March.

gloss: Someone who shoots with a bow and arrows.
examples: The *archer* hit the center of the target twice.
Medieval *archers* could fire ten arrows a minute.
She's the best *archer* on the college team.

gloss: A collection of old documents or records, or the place where they are kept.
examples: The letters are in the university *archive*.
He spent a week in the city *archives*.
The newspaper put its whole *archive* online.
contrast: The ch sounds like k: AR-kyve.

gloss: Someone whose job is to look after historical records.
examples: The *archivist* found the original blueprints for us.
Two *archivists* are scanning the photo collection.
She trained as a librarian and became an *archivist*.

gloss: Strong, passionate feeling for something or someone.
examples: He defended the project with real *ardor*.
Her *ardor* for the cause never cooled.
The crowd's *ardor* faded as the game dragged on.
contrast: Americans write *ardor*; the British write *ardour*.

gloss: A colorless gas that does not react with other substances, used in light bulbs and welding.
examples: The bulb is filled with *argon* instead of air.
*Argon* makes up about one percent of the atmosphere.
The welder uses *argon* to shield the joint.

gloss: An angry disagreement, or a reason given to support an opinion.
examples: They had a loud *argument* in the parking lot.
That's the strongest *argument* against the plan.
Both *arguments* sounded reasonable to me.

gloss: A member of the highest social class, usually by birth.
examples: The house was built by a French *aristocrat*.
Many *aristocrats* lost their land after the revolution.
He dresses like an *aristocrat* on a small salary.
contrast: Americans stress the second syllable, uh-RIS-tuh-krat; the British often say A-ris-tuh-krat.

gloss: A large fleet of warships, or any big group of vehicles moving together.
examples: An *armada* of fishing boats filled the harbor.
The Spanish *armada* sailed in 1588.
Two *armadas* of trucks brought in supplies.

gloss: A small American animal covered with hard bony plates.
examples: An *armadillo* was digging up the flower bed.
*Armadillos* are common all over Texas.
The dog barked at an *armadillo* under the porch.

gloss: Weapons and military equipment, especially of a country or a ship.
examples: The treaty limits *armaments* on both sides.
The ship's main *armament* is a pair of deck guns.
Spending on *armaments* rose again last year.

gloss: A strip of cloth worn around the upper arm as a sign or marker.
examples: The team wore black *armbands* for their old coach.
The captain's *armband* is bright yellow.
Volunteers were given an orange *armband* at the gate.

gloss: An agreement between enemies to stop fighting.
examples: The *armistice* took effect at eleven in the morning.
Both sides broke the *armistice* within a week.
Earlier *armistices* had collapsed in a matter of days.

gloss: A building where weapons are stored, often also used by the National Guard.
examples: The concert is at the old *armory* downtown.
Rifles were locked in the *armory* overnight.
Several *armories* have been turned into museums.
contrast: Americans write *armory*; the British write *armoury*.

gloss: The part of a seat that you rest your arm on.
examples: We fought over the *armrest* the whole flight.
The chair's *armrests* adjust up and down.
He fell asleep with his elbow on the *armrest*.

gloss: The use of scented plant oils to help someone relax or feel better.
examples: The spa offers massage and *aromatherapy*.
She swears by *aromatherapy* for headaches.
*Aromatherapy* candles are on sale this week.

gloss: The state of being excited, alert, or sexually stimulated.
examples: Caffeine raises your level of *arousal*.
The study measured *arousal* by heart rate.
Fear and *arousal* look similar in the brain.

gloss: The notes of a chord played one after another instead of together.
examples: The song opens with a soft guitar *arpeggio*.
She practices scales and *arpeggios* every morning.
Play the *arpeggio* a little slower this time.
contrast: The double g sounds like j: ar-PEH-jee-oh.

gloss: The court hearing where a person is formally charged and enters a plea.
examples: His *arraignment* is set for Tuesday morning.
She pleaded not guilty at the *arraignment*.
The judge handled a dozen *arraignments* before lunch.
contrast: The g is silent: uh-RAYN-munt.

gloss: A plan agreed with someone, or the way things are placed.
examples: We have an *arrangement* about who picks up the kids.
The new seating *arrangement* works much better.
Travel *arrangements* will be emailed to you.

gloss: Money that is owed and should already have been paid.
examples: He's three months in *arrears* on the rent.
The company paid off its *arrears* in June.
Interest is charged on any *arrears*.
contrast: *Arrears* is always plural in form — there is no singular *arrear*.

gloss: The sharp point fixed to the front of an arrow.
examples: He found a stone *arrowhead* in the creek bed.
The museum has a case full of *arrowheads*.
The *arrowhead* was chipped from black glass.

gloss: A very poisonous chemical element found in some rocks and water.
examples: The well water tested high for *arsenic*.
In old mysteries, someone is always poisoned with *arsenic*.
*Arsenic* was once used in green paint.

gloss: An object made by people, especially an old one studied by historians.
examples: The *artifact* dates from about 800 BC.
Thousands of *artifacts* were dug up at the site.
Every *artifact* in the case is labeled.
contrast: Americans write *artifact*; the British write *artefact*.

gloss: An animal with a hard outer shell and jointed legs, such as an insect, spider, or crab.
examples: A lobster is an *arthropod*, not a fish.
*Arthropods* make up most of the animal species on Earth.
The chapter covers one *arthropod* group per page.

gloss: An artificial sweetener used instead of sugar in diet drinks and foods.
examples: Diet soda is sweetened with *aspartame*.
She avoids anything with *aspartame* in it.
The label lists *aspartame* as the third ingredient.

gloss: One part or side of a situation or subject.
examples: The legal *aspect* of the deal worries me most.
We looked at every *aspect* of the proposal.
There are *aspects* of the job she still enjoys.

gloss: A tall, slender tree with pale bark and leaves that shake in the wind.
examples: A single *aspen* grew by the fence.
The *aspens* turn bright gold in September.
We hiked through a grove of *aspens*.

gloss: A strong wish to achieve something in life.
examples: Her *aspiration* is to run her own clinic.
The survey asked teenagers about their *aspirations*.
He gave up his *aspiration* of playing professionally.

gloss: Someone who murders an important person, often for money or politics.
examples: The *assassin* was caught two blocks away.
Police believe there were two *assassins*.
He plays a retired *assassin* in the movie.

gloss: A man who serves in a state assembly in the United States.
examples: The *assemblyman* voted against the budget.
Three *assemblymen* co-sponsored the bill.
She wrote to her *assemblyman* about the bridge.
contrast: Irregular plural: one *assemblyman*, two *assemblymen*.

gloss: Formal agreement to a plan or request.
examples: The board gave its *assent* to the merger.
He nodded in silent *assent*.
Nothing moves forward without her *assent*.
contrast: *Assent* sounds exactly like *ascent* (a climb upward).

gloss: A confident statement that something is true, given without proof.
examples: That *assertion* is not supported by the data.
He repeated his *assertion* that the vote was fair.
The article is full of unchecked *assertions*.

gloss: A judgment about how good, valuable, or serious something is.
examples: Her *assessment* of the risk turned out to be right.
Students take a reading *assessment* twice a year.
The two *assessments* reached opposite conclusions.

gloss: The process of becoming part of a larger group, or of taking something in fully.
examples: The book traces the *assimilation* of Italian immigrants.
*Assimilation* of the new material takes practice.
She resisted complete *assimilation* into the new culture.

gloss: Someone you work with, especially a junior partner or a store employee.
examples: Ask a sales *associate* to open the case for you.
He's a junior *associate* at a law firm.
Two of her old *associates* testified against her.
contrast: The noun ends in -see-ut (uh-SOH-see-ut); the verb ends in -see-ayt (uh-SOH-see-ayt).

gloss: A promise meant to make someone feel confident that something will happen.
examples: He gave us his *assurance* that the roof would hold.
The airline's *assurances* meant nothing by then.
We need written *assurance* before we sign.

gloss: A garden flower with a yellow center and many thin purple, pink, or white petals.
examples: A single purple *aster* was still blooming.
She planted *asters* along the driveway.
The *asters* last well into October here.

gloss: An eye condition that makes vision blurry because the eye is not evenly curved.
examples: The exam showed mild *astigmatism* in one eye.
*Astigmatism* is corrected with special lenses.
He has enough *astigmatism* to need glasses for driving.

gloss: A liquid put on the skin to tighten it and dry up oil.
examples: She wipes her face with an *astringent* every night.
Most drugstore *astringents* contain alcohol.
Use a gentle *astringent* if your skin is dry.

gloss: Someone who claims to predict events from the positions of the stars and planets.
examples: An *astrologer* wrote the column in the back of the magazine.
Kings once kept *astrologers* at court.
She paid an *astrologer* to read her chart.

gloss: The branch of science that studies the physical nature of stars and other objects in space.
examples: She has a doctorate in *astrophysics*.
*Astrophysics* explains how stars burn and die.
He teaches *astrophysics* to first-year students.
contrast: It ends in -s but takes a singular verb: *Astrophysics is hard*, not *are hard*.

gloss: The condition of two sides not matching each other.
examples: There's a slight *asymmetry* in almost every face.
The *asymmetry* of the design is deliberate.
Critics pointed to the *asymmetry* of the deal.

gloss: The belief that no god exists.
examples: He turned to *atheism* in his twenties.
The book is a defense of *atheism*.
*Atheism* is more common among younger Americans.

gloss: Physical strength, speed, and skill in sports.
examples: Her *athleticism* makes up for her height.
Scouts praised his raw *athleticism*.
The play showed real *athleticism*.

gloss: Something done to make up for a wrong you have committed.
examples: He spent years in *atonement* for that mistake.
The novel is about guilt and *atonement*.
She offered the money as *atonement*.

gloss: The wasting away of a body part or a skill from lack of use.
examples: Weeks in bed caused serious muscle *atrophy*.
The scan showed *atrophy* in part of the brain.
He warned about the *atrophy* of basic math skills.

gloss: A person who attacks someone, or a player whose job is to score.
examples: She described her *attacker* to the police.
The *attackers* fled in a white van.
Their best *attacker* was out with a knee injury.

gloss: The reaching of a goal or a level, especially in education.
examples: Educational *attainment* has risen in the county.
The report tracks *attainment* in reading and math.
Pay is tied to the *attainment* of clear targets.

gloss: An act of trying to do something.
examples: Her first *attempt* at bread was a disaster.
He passed the test on his third *attempt*.
Both *attempts* to restart the engine failed.

gloss: Someone whose job is to help or serve people in a particular place.
examples: The flight *attendant* brought us extra water.
Ask the parking *attendant* where to leave the car.
Two *attendants* were on duty at the pool.

gloss: A quality or feature that belongs to someone or something.
examples: Patience is his best *attribute*.
The database stores three *attributes* for each user.
Size is not the only *attribute* that matters here.
contrast: The noun is A-trih-byoot; the verb moves the stress: uh-TRIH-byoot.

gloss: The act of saying who created something or what caused it.
examples: The photo was used without *attribution*.
*Attribution* of the attack took weeks.
The license requires *attribution* to the original author.

gloss: A steady loss of people or strength over time.
examples: The company cut staff through *attrition*, not layoffs.
It became a war of *attrition*.
Nurse *attrition* is the hospital's biggest problem.

gloss: The person who runs an auction and takes the bids.
examples: The *auctioneer* talked faster than I could follow.
Two *auctioneers* took turns on the platform.
The *auctioneer* banged the gavel and moved on.

gloss: Bold nerve, either brave or rude.
examples: He had the *audacity* to ask for a raise that week.
I admired the *audacity* of the plan.
She answered with real *audacity*.

gloss: A feeling or quality that seems to surround a person or place.
examples: There's an *aura* of calm about her.
The old courthouse has an *aura* of authority.
Some people claim to see *auras* around others.

gloss: The support and protection of an organization that backs an event or program.
examples: The talks were held under the *auspices* of the United Nations.
The clinic runs under the *auspices* of the state health department.
Under her *auspices*, the festival doubled in size.
contrast: Used almost only in the phrase *under the auspices of*.

gloss: A government policy of cutting spending sharply, or a very plain way of living.
examples: Years of *austerity* left the schools crumbling.
The new *austerity* measures hit pensions hardest.
They lived in wartime *austerity* for most of a decade.

gloss: The quality of being genuine and not a copy or an act.
examples: An expert confirmed the painting's *authenticity*.
Fans respond to her *authenticity*.
The restaurant is praised for the *authenticity* of its food.

gloss: The fact of being the person who wrote or created something.
examples: The *authorship* of the play is still disputed.
He never claimed *authorship* of the memo.
Journals now require clear *authorship* for every paper.

gloss: A lifelong condition that affects how a person communicates and relates to others.
examples: Their son was diagnosed with *autism* at three.
The school has a program for kids with *autism*.
Research on *autism* has changed a lot in twenty years.

gloss: A country or system in which one person holds all the power.
examples: The country slid from democracy into *autocracy*.
Modern *autocracies* still hold elections of a kind.
He warned that the reform would create an *autocracy*.

gloss: A camera system that sharpens the image by itself.
examples: The *autofocus* struggles in low light.
Turn off *autofocus* when you shoot through glass.
This lens has fast, quiet *autofocus*.

gloss: A famous person's signature, kept as a souvenir.
examples: He got the pitcher's *autograph* on a baseball.
She collects *autographs* from old movie stars.
The line for *autographs* stretched around the block.
